segments.title: Creed Taylor's control-room methods and the Quincy session personnel
segments.summary: Laws explains Creed Taylor's habit of working through intermediaries and phones. Brown lists the large cast on Walking in Space and Paul Desmond's From the Hot Afternoon.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: Crying Song, the Gary McFarland date and guitarist Sam Brown
segments.summary: Brown dates Crying Song to September 1969. Laws identifies a garbled name in the discography as guitarist Sam Brown.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: Ron Carter, George Benson, Mongo's Stone Soul and Ernie Wilkins
segments.summary: Brown reads through late 1969 and early 1970s dates; Laws recalls the Ernie Wilkins session playing sax and flute.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: The Afro-Classic album and Amazing Grace: fathers' reactions
segments.summary: Brown shows his copy of Afro-Classic and tells how his father responded to Amazing Grace. Laws says his own father cried on hearing it.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: Choosing material for Afro-Classic with Creed Taylor and Don Sebesky
segments.summary: Laws describes choosing the Bach Passacaglia, Love Story, a Mozart sonata and Fire and Rain, with Creed Taylor's suggestions and Sebesky's arrangements.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: The Afro-Classic Ensemble and its drummer Freddie Waits
segments.summary: Brown opens the LP; Laws recalls his first group, the Afro-Classic Ensemble, with Ron Carter and Freddie Waits.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: Choosing players for Van Gelder's studio; David Friedman
segments.summary: Laws says Creed and Rudy Van Gelder were picky about players. He brought his band, Freddie Waits, Bob James, Ron Carter and vibraphonist Dave Friedman.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: The flute effects device that sounded like bassoon and flute
segments.summary: Laws describes using an analog octave-divider that gave a combined bassoon-and-flute sound on Passacaglia.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: Fred Alston and Chick Corea's trio for bassoon, piano and flute
segments.summary: Laws recalls Fred Alston on bassoon and Chick Corea's all-classical trio on Laws' Cause. He criticizes the intonation and recorded sound.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: Changing the flute's sound in the 1970s
segments.summary: Brown notes the quest for new sounds after Hendrix. Laws says he prizes a pure flute sound but will experiment if he keeps control.

segments.chapter: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
segments.title: The NEA downplaying his classical background
segments.summary: Brown asks why the Jazz Masters presentation downplayed Laws's classical training. Laws says he had not thought about it, and they agree he bridged both worlds.

segments.title: What the NEA Jazz Masters award means; arts funding cuts
segments.summary: Laws says he has come to appreciate the award and recognition for improvisation. They discuss threatened funding for the NEA program.

segments.title: Nationalism, government and music as a unifying force
segments.summary: Laws argues that nationalism causes conflict and that one government would end it. He distinguishes music from government, and Brown calls music a unifying force.

segments.title: The shepherd analogy for selfishness and family leadership
segments.summary: Laws retells an article about two kinds of shepherd to explain selfishness, bad behavior and how families and societies handle rebels.

segments.title: Leaders who serve themselves; corporate power
segments.summary: Laws and Brown criticize self-serving politicians and executives, citing the Bell scandal, Citizens United and university tuition protests.

segments.title: Human rulership cannot be the solution
segments.summary: Laws says humans are unqualified to rule and promises to give Brown literature with the solution, citing Libya and Egypt.

segments.title: Opening of day two and corrections
segments.summary: Brown opens day two on March 5, 2011, corrects the name Nasheed Waits and returns to Laws's siblings.

segments.title: The Laws siblings
segments.summary: Laws goes through his siblings, among them Blanche, Johnny, Eloise, Ronnie, Charlotte, Debra and Donna, and their musical careers.

segments.title: The family ensemble, Debra's talent and Ronnie today
segments.summary: Laws recalls bringing family members into performances, Debra's gifts, and his view of Ronnie's gigging.

segments.title: His children, his son's grandfather Roy Gaines, and the Philippines
segments.summary: Laws talks about his daughter Ashley, who writes and sings, and his son Sky, whose grandfather is bluesman Roy Gaines. They end with a present from the Philippines.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Count Basie's Afrique, Oliver Nelson and Tom McIntosh
segments.summary: Laws does not recall Mingus but remembers recording with Count Basie via Oliver Nelson. He talks about Nelson, J. J. Johnson and Tom McIntosh.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Quincy Jones dates, living in New York and the Academy Awards
segments.summary: Brown reviews Smackwater Jack and other Quincy dates. Laws says he lived in New York until buying in Los Angeles in 1977-78 and recalls Quincy getting him on the Academy Awards.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Hermeto Pascoal and the bobcat
segments.summary: Laws remembers Hermeto Pascoal mostly because of the huge bobcat in his New York apartment. He links him with Airto and Jobim circle.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Melvin Sparks session
segments.summary: Brown mentions a Melvin Sparks date at Van Gelder's; Laws does not know him.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Gil Scott-Heron's Pieces of a Man
segments.summary: Brown says Pieces of a Man influenced his generation. Laws recalls playing flute on The Revolution Will Not Be Televised.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: New York studio life: commercials and the pension
segments.summary: Laws describes cycling between sessions with his flute and doing many TV commercials. The jingle work now provides a union pension, unlike many older musicians.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Recording La Mer with Bernstein and other orchestral dates
segments.summary: Laws recalls recording La Mer with the New York Philharmonic under Bernstein and a Gluck solo with Columbia Masterworks.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Playing live with Gil Scott-Heron
segments.summary: Laws says the Gil Scott-Heron track was cut live, that he knew little of Scott-Heron, and that Brown sees the album as touchstone of his generation.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: A recent track with Stevie Wonder
segments.summary: Laws describes playing on Stevie Wonder's recent record and being struck by Stevie's musicality, including a Giant Steps jam with Herbie Hancock.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Always at the right place at the right time
segments.summary: Brown and Laws reflect that Laws keeps landing in sessions that become historic, such as Gil Scott-Heron and the CTI compendium.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Kenny Burrell's God Bless the Child and working with Don Sebesky
segments.summary: Laws believes Don Sebesky got him on Kenny Burrell's date. He praises Sebesky's orchestral arranging, including First Light, and describes calling to thank him.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Reaction to the Rite of Spring album
segments.summary: Brown says Laws's Rite of Spring album astonished him and James Newton. Laws says he did not understand the fuss and notes Sebesky's role.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Sebesky writing parts in the car; Slide Hampton and circular breathing
segments.summary: Laws says Sebesky wrote the Rite of Spring and Passacaglia parts in pencil outside Van Gelder's studio. He compares Slide Hampton, who taught him circular breathing.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Bridging concert music and jazz on Rite of Spring
segments.summary: Brown notes Fauré and Syrinx on the album. Laws says it was only snippets from Stravinsky treated with improvisation and he would play it more dramatically now.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Rudy Van Gelder's flute sound compared with Atlantic engineers
segments.summary: Laws praises Rudy Van Gelder for capturing the flute better than anyone, contrasts engineers at Atlantic, and mentions Phil Ramone and Van Gelder's white gloves.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Rudy Van Gelder's microphone setup
segments.summary: Laws describes the close single Shure mic on his mouthpiece, the isolation booth, and Van Gelder's secrecy about equipment.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Rudy's bluntness, Creed's diplomacy and consoling Rudy
segments.summary: Laws recalls Rudy Van Gelder shutting down a session over a visiting engineer, contrasts him with Creed Taylor, and recalls consoling him after his wife died.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Freddie Hubbard and the First Light overdubs
segments.summary: Laws says he met Freddie Hubbard through CTI in 1969, and on First Light overdubbed solos onto a finished rhythm track.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: The Mingus Let My Children Hear Music credit
segments.summary: Brown notes Lord lists Laws on a 1971 Mingus date. Laws suggests he played a Sebesky chart without knowing it was Mingus's record.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: George Benson, guitarists and the CTI All-Stars tour of Japan
segments.summary: Laws praises George Benson and recalls his Crying Song work. He tells of the first Japan tour and the Hank Crawford and Freddie Hubbard arguments on the bus.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Creed Taylor's background and singular vision
segments.summary: Laws learns from Creed Taylor that he played trombone and grew up in Virginia, and says Creed stuck to his own vision.

segments.chapter: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
segments.title: Creed Taylor's confrontation with Bill Evans on tour
segments.summary: Laws recalls Creed Taylor and saxophonist Bill Evans having a heated exchange on the recent European CTI tour.

segments.title: Weather Report's I Sing the Body Electric and Zawinul
segments.summary: Laws recalls the Columbia session for Zawinul's Unknown Soldier and praises Zawinul and Wayne Shorter as composers.

segments.title: Meeting Wayne Shorter in Panama
segments.summary: Laws describes visiting Panama, where he played with singer Luba Mason and met Wayne Shorter.

segments.title: Why singing matters: George Benson, Nat King Cole and Laws's own vocals
segments.summary: Brown compares George Benson to Nat King Cole. Laws says he tried to sing but has no hope, and that vocals bridge the gap to audiences.

segments.title: The last Atlantic record: Motherless Child with John Murtaugh
segments.summary: Laws explains that his CTI deal required one more Atlantic album, a strings-only record arranged by John Murtaugh.

segments.title: Jackie Cain's Time & Love
segments.summary: Brown names a Jackie Cain CTI record; Laws barely remembers it.

segments.title: Quincy Jones's You've Got It Bad Girl and Toots Thielemans
segments.summary: Brown reviews the Quincy album's personnel, including Stevie Wonder, Bob James and Toots Thielemans. Laws says he played often with Toots.

segments.title: Charles Earland's session and Lee Morgan's death
segments.summary: Laws recalls that the Charles Earland session was the day Lee Morgan was shot, and learned of it from Harold Mabern.

segments.title: A tangent about domestic disputes and the courts
segments.summary: Laws goes off on an extended opinion about women, judges, and being trapped in his own house.

segments.title: Randy Weston's Blue Moses and Laws's first trip to Africa
segments.summary: Laws recalls playing Blue Moses and says Randy Weston led to his first trip to Tangier. He describes hearing North African flute players while sick.

segments.title: Bobby Hutcherson and recording logistics
segments.summary: Brown recounts Gil Scott-Heron's Free Will and Bobby Hutcherson's Natural Illusions sessions. Laws recalls driving to Englewood Cliffs and seeing Hutcherson in Pasadena.

segments.title: Woodwind colleagues Romeo Penque and George Marsh
segments.summary: Laws talks about section players Romeo Penque, Phil Bodner, Jerry Dodgion and George Marsh.

segments.title: Airto's Free
segments.summary: Laws doesn't recall the session but praises Airto's ability to make sound from anything.

segments.title: The CTI Carnegie Hall concerts promoted by New Audiences
segments.summary: Laws explains that New Audiences hired the CTI band to play Carnegie Hall for several consecutive years.

segments.title: Morning Star and Amazing Grace
segments.summary: Brown praises Morning Star. Laws explains the title tune came from a Mongo pianist and he recorded Amazing Grace for his father, correcting Don Sebesky's lush approach.

segments.title: What Do You Think of This World Now, sung by Debra
segments.summary: Laws describes the message song with Debra at sixteen and plans to re-record it with her.

segments.title: Sky Dive with Freddie Hubbard and Gabor Szabo
segments.summary: Brown cites Sky Dive and Povo as classics. Laws does not remember Gabor Szabo's date.

segments.title: His last saxophone date: Quincy's The Color Purple
segments.summary: Laws says he stopped doubling around 1985-86, when Quincy had him bring his tenor to The Color Purple. Quincy's memory of everyone's name impressed him.

segments.title: Ron Carter and the Miles Davis quintet
segments.summary: Laws praises Ron Carter's supportive playing and the Miles Davis quintet with Herbie Hancock, Tony Williams and Wayne Shorter. He recounts Carter's reaction to his chart on Shades of Light.

segments.title: Eric Gale's Forecast and the January 1973 Carnegie Hall concert
segments.summary: Brown reads through Eric Gale's Forecast and the 1973 Carnegie Hall concert, with Dave Miller on bassoon.

segments.title: Grover Washington Jr.'s accidental break at CTI
segments.summary: Laws tells how Grover Washington Jr. got his chance when a no-show left the rhythm section without a saxophonist.

segments.title: Don Sebesky's Giant Box and Stanley Turrentine's last record
segments.summary: Laws recalls Giant Box with Sebesky arranging aggressively. He tells of learning of Stanley Turrentine's stroke on the way to Bermuda and recording I Should Care for free.

segments.title: McCoy Tyner's Song of the New World and Fly with the Wind; Orrin Keepnews
segments.summary: Laws had forgotten playing Afro-Blue on Song of the New World but remembers Fly with the Wind. He found Orrin Keepnews easy to work with.

segments.title: Norman Connors's Love from the Sun
segments.summary: Brown lists personnel on Norman Connors's all-star record; Laws does not recall it.

segments.title: Milt Jackson's Goodbye
segments.summary: Brown names the Milt Jackson CTI quintet date; Laws can't recall it.

segments.title: Freddie Hubbard's Polar AC
segments.summary: Laws loves Polar AC, where Freddie played superbly. Brown lists Bob James and Sebesky arrangements.

segments.title: Quincy Jones's Body Heat
segments.summary: Laws remembers Body Heat only vaguely. Brown praises its tracks and Bernard Ighner's Everything Must Change.

segments.title: Bill Evans's Symbiosis
segments.summary: Laws recalls working with Claus Ogerman but not the Bill Evans date, which he did not know about.

segments.title: In the Beginning and Clare Fischer's arrangements
segments.summary: Laws describes Clare Fischer's arrangements, free opening and Fischer's diabetes during the session at Van Gelder's.

segments.title: Other tracks on In the Beginning; Come Ye Disconsolate for his mother
segments.summary: Brown and Laws go through Restoration, Reconciliation, Mean Lean, Gymnopedie and Come Ye Disconsolate, which he recorded for his mother.

segments.title: How Laws played Moment's Notice
segments.summary: Laws cannot explain his Coltrane-like solo on Moment's Notice, saying he practiced changes and did one take.

segments.title: The Airegin duet with Steve Gadd and Giant Steps
segments.summary: Laws describes the flute-and-drums Airegin, the octave divider, and wishes he could redo it. He has not recorded Giant Steps.

segments.title: Arif Mardin's Flight
segments.summary: Brown mentions a one-tune session on Arif Mardin's date; Laws doesn't remember it.

segments.title: Joe Farrell and missing the original Return to Forever recordings
segments.summary: Laws praises reedman Joe Farrell and says he played Chick's new tunes at the Village Vanguard but record-company issues kept him off the recording.

segments.title: Playing with Chick Corea at the new Yoshi's
segments.summary: Brown recalls hearing Laws, Chick, Eddie Gomez and Airto open the new Yoshi's in San Francisco. Laws praises the hall.

segments.title: Norman Connors, Chet Baker, Ron Carter and Patrice Rushen dates
segments.summary: Brown lists further 1974-75 sessions and Laws recalls few of them, mentioning dating Patrice Rushen.

segments.title: Alice Coltrane and Jaco Pastorius
segments.summary: Brown lists Alice Coltrane's date and Jaco's Used to Be a Cha Cha. Laws describes the outtake and Jaco's flexible thumb, from the trip to Havana.

segments.title: The 1975 San Francisco Concert and Betty Carter
segments.summary: Laws recalls the Paramount Theater concert with Bob James arrangements and Betty Carter opening. He admires Carter and her duets with Ray Charles.

segments.title: Blossom Dearie and Freddie Hubbard's Windjammer
segments.summary: Brown mentions Blossom Dearie and Freddie Hubbard's Windjammer; Laws recalls Rock Me Arms and Bob James's arrangements.

segments.title: Romeo and Juliet and moving to CBS
segments.summary: Laws says Romeo and Juliet sold modestly until Say It with Silence boosted it. He chose CBS for its international marketing.

segments.title: Tape break and Gary King on bass
segments.summary: The recording is interrupted and resumes mid-sentence with a remark about Bob James's rhythm players, including Gary King.

segments.title: Bob James albums and the number of Laws's recordings
segments.summary: Laws says he does not hear most of his sideman records. They joke about 333 sessions.

segments.title: Fly with the Wind, Bill Fischer and Orrin Keepnews
segments.summary: Laws describes the challenge of McCoy Tyner's fiery playing on Fly with the Wind at Fantasy and praises Orrin Keepnews for staying out of the way. He contrasts Joel Dorn.

segments.title: Lalo Schifrin and speaking Spanish
segments.summary: Laws recalls a UCLA event with Lalo Schifrin where they spoke Spanish.

segments.title: Helen Merrill session at Riverside
segments.summary: Laws recalls a Helen Merrill session at the Riverside studios and Mongo's last records there.

segments.title: John Lewis and the Monterey Jazz Festival
segments.summary: Laws recalls playing with John Lewis in New York and discovers a Monterey Jazz Festival video he had forgotten.

segments.title: Creed Taylor losing artists and why Laws left CTI
segments.summary: Laws explains that CTI had financial trouble and big labels lured artists with signing fees, though he never received such money from CTI.

segments.title: Offers from labels and the Tentmakers management group
segments.summary: Laws describes offers from ABC, Atlantic, Fantasy, Warner and CBS, and advice from Benny Golson's management group Tentmakers. He tells how he broke with manager Ron Nadel at Montreux.

segments.title: Say It with Silence and its vocal hit False Faces
segments.summary: Laws describes Say It with Silence as his best-selling album, with mostly his own compositions and arrangements for strings.

segments.title: Learning to write for strings in Don Sebesky's class
segments.summary: Laws explains that he learned to write economical string arrangements in Sebesky's class, where he sat next to Valerie Simpson.

segments.title: Land of Passion and writing lyrics
segments.summary: Laws describes Land of Passion, its Grammy nomination, his duets with Johnny and Debra, and lyrics as the title poem.

segments.title: Havana Jam in Cuba
segments.summary: Laws describes visiting Havana for Havana Jam, the austerity, hearing Weather Report with Jaco Pastorius live.

segments.title: The Family album
segments.summary: Laws recalls the success of Family, with his arrangements and constant orders for the record.

segments.title: The Family Carnegie Hall concert and Billy Taylor's praise
segments.summary: Laws recalls the Carnegie Hall concert with his siblings and a big band and Billy Taylor's compliments.

segments.title: Bill Fischer as arranger
segments.summary: Brown and Laws identify Bill Fischer as arranger of McCoy Tyner albums; Laws says Fischer now has Alzheimer's.

segments.title: Victor Feldman's direct-to-disc Secret of the Andes
segments.summary: Laws recalls his first direct-to-disc recording, with Harvey Mason and others.

segments.title: Stepping back from recording to raise his children
segments.summary: Laws says he stopped recording around 1985 when his children were born.

segments.title: Brazilian Romance with Sarah Vaughan
segments.summary: Laws recalls Sergio Mendes calling him for Sarah Vaughan's record and notes three singers died after he played with them.

segments.title: Sessions from 1990s: Lorber, Hancock, Lainie Kazan, Pat Williams
segments.summary: Brown reads through later credits and Laws remembers some, such as Lainie Kazan and Pat Williams's Sinatraland.

segments.title: Quincy Jones's Basie and Beyond, Juke Joint and Eugene Maslov
segments.summary: Brown lists Quincy's Basie and Beyond. Laws mentions Juke Joint's dedication and Eugene Maslov.

segments.title: Playing with Chick Corea on The Ultimate Adventure
segments.summary: Laws says playing with Chick Corea is always a challenge and that he learns from Chick's spontaneous creativity.

segments.title: Terry Gibbs's Finding the Groove for $500
segments.summary: Laws laughs that he was paid $500 for the entire Terry Gibbs record.

segments.title: Kenny Burrell at Yoshi's and the end of the discography
segments.summary: Brown covers Kenny Burrell's Yoshi's recording and the discography ends in 2008. Laws warns that he cannot remember everything.

segments.title: Current travel and how bookings are handled
segments.summary: Laws describes upcoming tours and travel plans and says his daughter helps process bookings through his website.

segments.title: Career arc, retirement security and upcoming projects
segments.summary: Laws says pensions and annuities mean he works by choice. He describes planned projects with Kamau Kenyatta and prefers not to overbook.

segments.title: The Tierney Sutton trio
segments.summary: Laws describes the cooperative trio with Tierney Sutton and Larry Koontz and how Kenny Burrell introduced them.

segments.title: Places he wants to play and possible concert-music projects
segments.summary: Laws names places he's never played and mentions a possible Japan project with pianist Yayoi Yoshida.

segments.title: Future dates with Chick Corea
segments.summary: Laws says Chick Corea always initiates their collaborations and recently emailed about doing something soon.

segments.title: Becoming a Jehovah's Witness
segments.summary: Brown notes the thanks to Jehovah on Land of Passion. Laws says he began studying after Juilliard and wants Brown to read his research on government.

segments.title: How his faith shapes lyrics
segments.summary: Laws says his faith affects his lyrics subliminally and describes the message song What Do You Think of This World Now.

segments.title: Religion, government and the solution
segments.summary: Laws argues conventional religion keeps people enslaved and that government is the central issue, pressing Brown to read his material.

segments.title: What music can and cannot do
segments.summary: Brown asks what wisdom music has given Laws. Laws says music brings friendships but does not govern moral behavior.

segments.title: Role models and parenting
segments.summary: They discuss modeling behavior and Laws's view of his father as an imperfect model.

segments.title: Closing: pointing to a greater model
segments.summary: Brown speaks of his granddaughter. Laws says he points away from himself to the ultimate model and urges Brown to read the material.
